analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run Medicare drug plan that negotiates prescription prices directly with drugmakers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and its Health subcommittees and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a nationally available prescription drug plan run directly by Medicare, competing alongside the private plans in Part D. Medicare would have to negotiate drug prices with manufacturers and push cheaper therapeutic equivalents where medically appropriate, with the savings used to fill the coverage gap (the "doughnut hole") for seniors. This would have ended the arrangement, set by the 2003 Medicare drug law, in which the government may not negotiate drug prices directly. The bill was referred to two House committees and then to Health subcommittees, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries. The bill would have created a nationally available, Medicare-run drug plan with premiums set the same everywhere, and directed the savings from negotiated prices toward filling the coverage gap. Any senior who found private Part D plans expensive or confusing could have enrolled at any time without a late-enrollment penalty.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries facing high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: It required the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer a Medicare-operated prescription drug plan available nationwide, in every region.

It required the Secretary to negotiate directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers over the purchase price of covered drugs and to use cost-saving strategies similar to those of the Department of Veterans Affairs, a federal buyer known for securing lower prices.

It directed that savings from the negotiated prices be used to extend coverage to beneficiaries who had fallen into the gap between their plan's initial coverage limit and the annual out-of-pocket threshold — the coverage gap known as the doughnut hole.
It allowed beneficiaries to switch into the Medicare-operated plan at any time, without the late-enrollment penalty that normally applies to Part D.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would have faced direct price negotiation from the government's largest drug buyer instead of the current ban on Medicare negotiating prices, and private Part D plan insurers, who would have competed against a low-cost public option backed by federal purchasing power.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private drug plan insurers

drawbacks.text: Giving the federal government a national drug plan with direct purchasing power concentrates enormous market power in one public buyer, which critics argued could crowd out private plans and, over time, pressure manufacturers to accept lower prices that might reduce investment in new medicines.

The plan's formulary powers were broad: it could encourage cheaper 'therapeutic equivalents' as long as medical necessity was determined by the prescribing physician, leaving room for disputes over which drugs seniors could access through the public plan.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit was real: allowing Medicare to compete with private Part D plans and use its bargaining power, the way the VA does, would likely have lowered drug costs for seniors and filled the "doughnut hole" coverage gap. The costs were modest: private plans would lose market share, and critics of government negotiation argue it could narrow the range of drugs available or slow drug development, though this bill let physicians determine medical necessity. Its main flaw was political rather than design: with two committee referrals and no cosponsor support beyond a handful of Democrats, it had no realistic path to a vote in a Congress where the 2003 prohibition on Medicare drug negotiation remained law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to their Health subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Introduced on April 26, 2007, the bill was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
Within days, both committees referred it to their Health subcommittees; no further action was ever taken.
The bill died at the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009, without receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prescription drug plan insurers and pharmaceutical manufacturers kept the status quo, including the legal ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices, which stood until repealed in 2010.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

for.name: Rep. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a Medicare-run drug plan with negotiated prices.

for.name: Rep. Joe Courtney
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as an original cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced and cosponsored only by Democrats, with 8 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, and it died in committee without ever reaching a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required Medicare to negotiate drug purchase prices and push cheaper therapeutic equivalents, ending the rule that the government may not negotiate. For ordinary people this could mean lower premiums and coverage of the doughnut hole; the industry's interest in blocking it ran against the public's.

industries.industry: Private Part D prescription drug plan insurers
industries.note: A nationally uniform, Medicare-run plan with negotiated prices would have competed directly with private Part D plans, likely drawing enrollees away. Insurers' stake in the bill ran against beneficiaries seeking a cheaper option.
